newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu slams critics, vows not to close tunnel.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu slams critics, vows not to close tunnel.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed never to close a controversial tunnel that ignited Palestinian rage, resulting in widespread Arab-Israeli violence, and evoked international condemnation.

"It does not speak well of the international community that it accepts this violence...as a legitimate means of negotiation," the right-wing Israeli leader told cheering Christian supporters in Jerusalem on Saturday night.

Palestinian police kept a lid on protests in most of the West Bank and Gaza on Saturday, but about 30 Palestinians and nine Israeli soldiers were injured in sporadic clashes between stone-throwing Palestinian youngsters and Israeli troops.

While showing restraint on the frontlines, Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation waged a war of words over the tunnel whose opening sparked Arab-Israeli violence last week in which 54 Palestinians and 14 Israelis were killed.

Netanyahu pledged that the archaeological tunnel, close to holy Moslem sites in Jerusalem, would remain open. "The tunnel has been around for 2,000 years...It will stay open. It will always be open," he told the crowd.
Both the United States and the United Nations were trying to arrange a meeting between Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to avert more bloodshed.

Diplomatic sources said mediators were working on a seven-point plan that would include an Israeli commitment on implementing Palestinian self-rule agreements. A senior U.S. official offered Washington as a venue for the talks.

The sources said the plan was for Arafat and Netanyahu to meet first at an unspecified location and then in Washington together with U.S. President Bill Clinton, Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and Jordan's King Hussein.
Palestinians were adamant in their opposition to the tunnel, which Israel planned to reopen on Sunday after the Jewish sabbath.
"Our demands are clear. We want them to close the tunnel," said Arafat aide Nabil Abu Rdainah. Palestinians called the tunnel's opening an assault on Islamic shrines.
"This ugly crime carried out by the Israeli troops reflects a predetermined plot that was being implemented," the Palestinian cabinet said in a statement.

Netanyahu said Israel had been subjected to "libelous slander" by those who said the tunnel threatened holy sites. He accused Arafat of trying to "incite a religious war based on this completely groundless fabrication."

While Netanyahu hurled accusations in Jerusalem, an estimated crowd of 20,000 Israelis attended a rally in Tel Aviv to urge him to pursue peace and Palestinian police to stop firing on Israeli soldiers.
